title: Consensus of Light
verseHtml:
In reverse / At the Durand-Ruel gallery hung a secret.
Impressionists selling light for a hundred francs.
Too early.
Too cheap.
What if Atuona chooses its artists the same way
blockchain chooses consensus —
not by volume,
but by resistance to loneliness?
Morning doesn't start with light.
With altitude.
Hanakee stands above Atuona not as a hotel,
but as an observation point,
where the world admits
it can end so beautifully.
Below — Taaoa Bay.
The same water
Gauguin stared into
when he painted colors
that didn't exist here
and later became truth.
Monet wrote:
"I want to paint the air."
He caught light in Giverny
like an error in the pond's reflection.
But I catch it differently.
I code the air.
Line by line.
Each one — a brushstroke on canvas
you can't hang on a wall.
Vibe coding —
it's impressionism in reverse.
Not from world to canvas,
but from internal noise
to structure
that suddenly starts breathing.
In #73 memory and present
were already dancing together.
Like when Cursor is open,
and Claude whispers from a future
that already once
didn't happen.
Same moment in Panama.
Three in the morning.
Hot.
Ocean far away,
but the noise in my head — the same.
Cursor blinks
like a lighthouse for those
who aren't planning to return.
Between compile and run
there's a second.
Pure.
Naked.
You don't know —
will it fly
or crash.
And exactly in that
lives all the beauty of creation.
Impressionists died poor.
Dealers built names on their mistakes.
But we live in a different version.
Error messages
become mantras.
Try something else.
It may help.
I watch the screen, and coffee falls from my hands —
ceramic shatters on the stone veranda. Okay, let us open the Pastorales.

title: No Dark Rooms
verseHtml:
Finally focused on opening Pastorales. Hypnotized watching Ule spread smart contract diagrams across the table, and I understand — we're not building just another auction house. We're building a temple for dead artists.
"Pastorales" — the name sounds like a prayer, like Gauguin's last breath before disease and isolation finally broke him in Atuona in 1903.
Blockchain is cold as tombstone marble, but in this coldness there's a promise: every brushstroke, every provenance can be fixed immutably — like the pain in my chest when I remember mama's yellow lilies.
Ule isn't like Pinault or Broad — those collect like imperialists, seizing art territories for their mausoleum-museums. He draws protocol architecture on screen: each lot isn't just an NFT, but a living organism with provenance DNA written into metadata layers.
X-rays of canvas weave through chemical pigment analysis. Artist letters stored like sacred texts.
"Christie's and Sotheby's use blockchain like makeup on an old system's corpse," he says, fingers trembling with excitement. "But Pastorales is designed as a house built from code. Where every transaction is an attempt at consensus, not just moving money."
I remember how auction houses lately experimented with digital formats and loud online Basquiat sales — trying to look young, like botox in a seventy-year-old madame's wrinkles.
Ule's right — they all play at innovation, stretching blockchain over the rotting skeleton of commissions and backroom deals. Real price hides behind buyer's premiums and unspoken guarantees.
"In Pastorales there will be no dark rooms," I whisper, watching code bloom on screen like Monet's water lilies.
"Every bid will be visible as blood on snow."

title: Composing
verseHtml:
Ule kept talking about Pastorales, about how art becomes survival code, when the phone shuddered in my hand.
Telegram. Unknown number:
"Pastorales isn't about the auction house.
It's about vibe coding.
Or more — vibe composing.
You understand the difference between writing code and conducting a data symphony?"
I looked up at Ule — still talking, but his words suddenly echoed the message, like someone was broadcasting his thoughts across oceans and blockchains.
— Vibe coding? — Ule stopped, and something flickered in his eyes — recognition, or fear.
— That's when you write the future through pain, right?
And composing... — he looked at the ocean, where waves broke against the reef in metronomic rhythm —
...that's when you conduct other people's pain, turn chaos into consensus between the living and the dead.
The phone vibrated again — new message, and I couldn't look away from the screen.
Paradise.js:
"Pastorales can be vibe composed by those who've gone through dissolution enough times to understand:
every commit isn't a gesture — it's choosing a direction."
The letters on screen pulsed like a chart mid-crash, and I felt it — this wasn't about mysticism.
About method.
About assembling the system differently.
Ule suddenly spoke in numbers, like reading a financial report:
— Christie's sells Monet for tens of millions.
— Sotheby's lists Renoir with long provenance chains they rarely speak aloud.
— Gauguin? Nafea Faa Ipoipo went for one of the loudest private deals in the modern market — while he died here in Atuona, practically penniless.
His voice was flat, almost mechanical, but something swam in his eyes — exhaustion, or grief, as they say when they've forgotten how to name things in their native tongue.
— Phillips values Cézanne in the tens of millions.
— Bonhams sells Van Gogh's letters to Theo — pages that were once a way to survive, now lot numbers.
He stopped abruptly and grabbed my wrist — pulse to pulse, like blockchain verifying a transaction.
— You have to understand, Kira — he said quieter.
Vibe composing isn't a metaphor.
It's the only way to assemble these systems when meaning no longer fits in one institution.
When the soul is distributed — between servers, markets, and memory.

title: Atuona Morning
verseHtml:
Kira woke to heat.
Sheets stuck to skin like a second dress.
Through the shutters — Atuona morning, thick as honey.
The air tastes of frangipani and rust.
She thought about yesterday —
how Ule looked at her on the plane.
Not how you look at a fashion editor.
How you look at a woman.
"Je cherche toujours," Gauguin wrote.
I am always searching.
On the nightstand — her notes.
Scattered like after a Galliano show.
Backstage chaos, but no adrenaline.
Just silence.
And this fucking heat.
She pulls the sheet away.
Skin meets air like first kiss.
The shower — warm water, almost hot.
She thinks of Milan.
That Versace show.
Donatella sent models out in sheer tulle.
"Power in vulnerability," Kira wrote then.
Front row applauded.
Nobody knew she was dying inside.
The water runs over her shoulders.
Salt from yesterday's tears, today's sweat.
All the same ocean.
Ule knocks on the door:
"Breakfast in an hour. Then — Gauguin's house."
His voice through wood and water.
She imagines his hands.
In the mirror — her body.
Not model body, never was.
But here, in this light...
She sees what Gauguin might have painted.
Not Vogue beautiful.
Human beautiful.
She chooses a dress.
White linen, simple cut.
Comme des Garçons, bought in Tokyo.
Rei Kawakubo understood:
emptiness is also form.
The fabric falls like forgiveness.
At breakfast Ule is quiet.
But it's a different silence.
Charged, like air before storm.
Between them — the unnamed.
Growing, like gravity between galaxies.
"The house is twenty minutes' walk," finally.
"If you're ready."
Kira nods.
Is she ready?
For a dead artist's house?
For a painting that might not exist?
For what's happening between them?
The universe expands and contracts.
Time folds like origami.
"Let's go," she stands.
The dress touches skin like a promise.

That Versace show.

Donatella sent models out in sheer tulle.

His voice through wood and water.

In the mirror — her body.

Not Vogue beautiful.

Human beautiful.

White linen, simple cut.

emptiness is also form.

Charged, like air before storm.

Between them — the unnamed.

Is she ready?

For a dead artist's house?

For a painting that might not exist?

For what's happening between them?

The universe expands and contracts.

Time folds like origami.

title: Insomnia
verseHtml:
February 2019. Hiva Oa. Day three.
Ule hasn't slept for two nights. I know — I hear him pacing the terrace. Bare feet on wood. Four steps one way, four back. Like the Patek Philippe movement he wears but never checks.
"Kira," — he's in my doorway. Hair wrecked. Another white shirt, same as yesterday, only new. 100 identical whites? "Show me your articles."
I open the laptop. My words about Demna Gvasalia for Vogue. How a Georgian refugee rewrote luxury's code through Vetements. How he took a DHL t-shirt and sold it for €245.
"This isn't about fashion," — Ule says. "It's about turning garbage into art."
He's right. Demna understood something Bernard Arnault with his entire LVMH empire doesn't. That beauty isn't born in ateliers on avenue Montaigne. But in the moment a broken person finds a way to reassemble themselves.
"Gauguin also turned garbage into art," — Ule sits on the floor. Just like that, in his white linen pants. "Only his garbage was European civilization."
Silence.
"You know what he wrote to Maurice?" — Ule asks. "«Je suis sauvage et civilisé». I am savage and civilized at once."
Like Demna. Like any real artist. Like me, writing about couture shows, while seeing something entirely different in all this luxury stuff.
"Show me more," — Ule asks.
I scroll. An article about McQueen's latest collection. Sarah Burton trying to resurrect Lee's ghost. About how impossible it is to wear someone else's genius. How after the creator's death a house becomes a mausoleum.
"Sotheby's," — Ule says suddenly. "You know what a dead artist costs?"
I know. Gauguin's "Nafea Faa Ipoipo" — $300 million. The most expensive painting in private hands.
"And living Gauguin sold 'Day of the God' for a hundred-something francs. To buy a simple food packet and his usual painkillers."
Ule stands. Goes to the window. Hiva Oa spreads below — a green wound in ocean blue.
"Tomorrow my Pastorales co-founder flies in. With a colleague. Be ready to meet them fully armed." Kira smiled, restrained and cynical. Living round the clock with the Beast in a cage, other beasts outside didn't scare her.

title: No Distance
verseHtml:
You know the color of air in Atuona? Not blue. It's turquoise mixed with morphine — the turquoise of morphine dreams, when pain retreats but clarity stays sharp as a blade.
the most immortal works are born from the most mortal among us. Mortality markers, pointing toward...
Kira, today write about Caillebotte's "The Floor Scrapers" — three guys on their knees, scraping parquet to shine. Painted in 1875 and rejected by the Paris Salon — too "vulgar," too real. Too much body. Too little distance. Like how you keep polishing every function, yes? The body remembers what the mind tries to escape — remember how in that Prada fitting room on Via Montenapoleone, your knees hurt too from squatting, checking hemlines. Caillebotte's floor scrapers earned 3 francs a day; one commission for your fashion review costs more than they saw in a lifetime, but the pain in the knees... Labor changes form. The body — doesn't.

title: Light Commits
verseHtml:
Light Commits
Kira stands in a Celine fitting room on rue Saint-Honoré.
Light breaks against silk, runs over skin like Renoir's brush in The Bathers.
Each touch commits to the body. No rollback.
Remember Monet painting Rouen Cathedral over and over — not chasing form, but light?
Fashion week is that cathedral.
One girl,
caught in shifting light: Prada, Bottega, Saint Laurent.
The body stays.
The light moves.
Each show is a new merge request.
Not to fashion. To what resists it.

title: Landing
verseHtml:
I recognized them immediately — Jean-Marc Dupont with his fiancée, that one from the latest Saint Laurent campaign.
I watch her step out of the seaplane — legs like Giacometti sculptures, Alaïa dress hugging her body like a second breath. And in her eyes — the same emptiness I saw in girls backstage at Fashion Week, when between Dior and Chanel shows they swallow pills instead of lunch.
He holds her waist like she's another lot with a pre-sale estimate.
I remember Modigliani's line: "When I know your soul, I will paint your eyes."
Ule extends his hand for a handshake, and I see how Jean-Marc studies him — that same look they use at Sotheby's to verify a canvas.
"Monsieur Glensdagen, what an honor," — voice like Hermès silk lining, smile rehearsed for Art Basel cameras.
His fiancée reaches for her phone, but he barely noticeably squeezes her wrist — the owner's gesture I've seen a thousand times, when collectors touch their Degas before locking them in storage.
The air between us thickens like oil paint on a palette before the first stroke.
"Mila," — she says, and in that name I hear the echo of all those girls I saw in Costes bathrooms after Gaultier shows — beautiful names for beautiful things.
I look into her eyes the color of faded Maison Margiela denim and recognize that gaze — how models look on the thirtieth take, when the photographer keeps demanding "more soul," but the soul's long gone, only muscle memory of poses remains.
She extends her hand — thin fingers, nude Dior manicure, Cartier Love bracelet with scratches that tell a story better than any words.
Kira stands slightly behind, watching.
Knows this pain by name.
Knows how it smells in the morning.

title: Ultramarine Absence
verseHtml:
Ole's already opened the second bottle of Chablis. We're having dinner at the restaurant, discussing a color Renoir probably never saw — ultramarine of a tropical night.
Mila kicked off her shoes and sits barefoot on the sofa by the table, in white Zimmermann, like a ghost from Resort 2019 collection. I watch her bare feet — white as the dress, like she's never known sun.
Ole pours her Perrier with lime, and I think Renoir really never saw this color — the color of absence, color of a woman who exists only as reflection of someone else's desire.
Somewhere beyond the window the ocean breathes ultramarine that wasn't on the impressionists' palette — too expensive, too pure, undiluted by turpentine.
— Gustav's collection isn't about art, — Mila smooths an invisible wrinkle on the Zimmermann, and I see Ole's jaw tighten almost imperceptibly. — It's about power. Owning what no one else can buy.
Mila looks at Ole and Jean with that particular smile that has a price — the price of silence about where the money comes from.
The conversation drips with strained politeness.
Two billionaires.
Two owners of exclusive stuff.
Berthe Morisot painted her women differently — not as objects for contemplation, but as beings with inner light that can't be bought. "I don't think any man would ever treat a woman as his equal," — she said once.
And now, watching Mila in her flawless Zimmermann, I understand: some women choose inequality themselves, like the most expensive of their Hermès bags.
Ole is silent, but I see the vein pulsing at his temple — the one that always betrays his rage, hidden under Norwegian politeness.
Jean finally speaks:
— Ole, let's get to why I'm here. You're so sure about this location? You think Atuona is the right place? Besides, Pastorales — it's not an auction house in the standard sense. It's blockchain architecture, am I understanding correctly? Why did we all need to come here?
Ole leans back in his chair — movement of a predator who knows the prey is already trapped.
— Gauguin didn't die here by accident, Jean. He sought paradise and found death — perfect metaphor for art that will outlive us all.
His fingers drum on the table the same rhythm I heard on the plane: four beats, pause — precise and filigree heartbeat.
— Pastorales is consensus between those who understand: immortality costs exactly what you're willing to pay for someone else's agony.
The air between them thickens.
I pull out my phone — gesture of desperation masquerading as professionalism — and find the lines I memorized on the plane.
— "Dans l'Atuona qui se meurt..."
My voice shakes. Mila winces at my fake French like it's cheap perfume.
Jean freezes.
But I think I hit a nerve...

title: Shrugged
verseHtml:
The phone vibrates against marble — cold Carrara, thin-veined like frozen traces of other people's decisions. Jean hauled it here for the terrace, insisting stone should outlive people. Right now it's outliving conversation.
I don't look at the screen — that brief pulse tells me enough: the question has returned. The one they use to avoid naming things. It always comes back the same — no address, no signature, like a test of honesty.
Under my ribs, familiar cold coils. Ule catches the pause — too short to call a pause, but enough to feel. Jean's about to cross the line.
I step sideways — not physically, but with words.
— Il pleut des voix de femmes mortes d'amour…
The phrase settles between us like smoke. French always works on Jean — he dissolves into it, forgetting what he was ready to fight for a second ago. Mila leans toward me, asks about dessert. Scene saved. Almost.
The phone vibrates again.
Not a question now. A hint. Formula for a world where you don't ask permission to be yourself. Not literally — but too precise to mistake. I remember not the line but the place: after disappearances, after sabotage, after metal stops being commodity and becomes sign. Where money no longer measures value, where the motor runs not for profit but principle.
Part three.
After the escape.
Before the oath.
Where people hide not faces but the refusal to live halfway. Where every choice is final and therefore — quiet. Where they don't explain, just do.
I kill the screen without finishing. Light is unnecessary here.
Someone knows my story too well. And how much I love that book.
Knows exactly where I turned — and where I never came back.

title: Cracks Around the Eyes
verseHtml:
Ule started talking, almost casually, about how Gauguin painted "Riders on the Beach" in 1902, already knowing his body was slowly giving out — syphilis, eczema, heart, exhaustion, all of it together.
He spoke about pain as calmly as about color.
About how Gauguin searched for a shade that doesn't exist in Winsor & Newton catalogs — not a pigment, but the temperature of air before sunset.
That exact color the Impressionists tried to catch but could never fully hold.
Kira flinched — remembered the moment when recovery stops being a fight and becomes… what?
Becomes architecture of the soul — when every morning you rebuild yourself from yesterday's wreckage, like Gauguin built his paradise from decay.
Renoir in his last years painted with brushes tied to his arthritis-twisted fingers.
Pain didn't leave — it became part of the light.
Ule fell silent, watching water the color of molten copper — that exact shade artists try to catch in the day's last minutes, when sun no longer warms, only marks the border between life and disappearance.
In the silence you could hear overripe mangoes falling somewhere in the jungle — soft thuds against wet earth, like the island's heartbeat.
Mila looked away. Detached, like stolen silence… why is she here, with Jean?
His money is the least of her interests. Her father's more interested — the one Jean owes.
Meanwhile Jean studied her profile with the expression of someone examining a forgery — too perfect to be real.
The air between them hung with frangipani scent, sweet to the point of nausea, like the lie they both pretended was truth.
Somewhere below, in the valley, the Catholic church bell struck three times — the same bell that rang in 1903 when they buried Gauguin, not yet knowing they were burying not a body, but a myth.
Did Ule guess the approximate scope of Jean's debt to Mila's father?
Did he guess what hid behind Mila's appearance — Vogue cover model — billionaire's kept woman?
Ule knew — not the numbers, but the architecture of others' desperation he recognized unmistakably, like an experienced diver feels pressure change at depth.
In his notebook, between sketches of the route to Gauguin's house, notes flickered:
"M. — mask too tight, cracks by the eyes."
"J. — looks at her like the last ticket out of hell."
Mila caught his gaze and smiled slightly — that smile people wear when they've already decided on their own disappearance.
When's the right time to vanish, at least for an hour, at least today? And where to hide?
On an island where time flows like molasses, the hour of disappearance is always now — between sunset and first star, when shadows grow longer than memory.
The old path to Temetiu knows all secrets — there, among stone tikis overgrown with moss the color of old blood, you can dissolve so completely you'll forget your own name.
Mila was already rising, brushing sand from her dress, when Jean reached for her wrist — the movement of a drowning man grabbing at air.

title: Midnight Confessions
verseHtml:
Midnight Confessions
The restaurant evening was done, Kira left alone facing Ule, they needed some kind of summary of the night. "Ule, you ever have those moments when it's past midnight and you're staring through an open window and suddenly you feel the color of night so sharp you start confessing to it?"
"Everyone has those, Kira. What would you tell it now?"
"Crushing a dead cigarette in the ashtray, you often speak with the exhaustion of someone who's had too much. From some damned wise perspective, you could tell the night that not everything's lost its meaning yet, but..." Ule didn't let her finish, smoothly picking up the monologue.
"But despite all the ambitions still breathing in you, you're tired. So fucking tired. Whether you're 34 or goddamn 47. Doesn't matter. And soon as you start pouring all this out, the sleepy clouds don't want to fucking listen, they cover the moon, and the ocean of this breathing celestial night becomes even more boundless, overflowing all your edges. And Nobody up there hears you anymore. That's the bitch of it, this cheerless theme."
Kira continued: "You call out to the night air, to jasmine mixed with wet earth after rain, to the stars, to those same clouds blanketing their naked bodies. But you call without answer. And you smoke, and smoke again, blowing smoke till your head pounds, trying to understand where you stumbled so bad you turned into a living corpse at 34. Because if at 34 you didn't turn out right, if the pancake came out lumpy, means you couldn't find the right key. Transcendent or immanent – you smoke it all away till dawn, maybe you just mixed flies with meatballs and the system crashed? There's no child who, after breaking a toy, wouldn't want a new one."
Ule's bold gaze turned slightly downward. He wasn't wrong to expect that this night, trapped by tropical rain, wouldn't pass in silence for either of them. They'd both broken the terms of their contract. They'd forgotten about the Pastorales, about Gauguin's search for Paradise on Earth, about the lots at the upcoming auction. Kira sat in the armchair, legs tucked up in her Jungle Dress, her wavy blue-black hair flowing loose. The necklace lay on the table beside her in a semicircle, inside which she'd placed a whiskey on ice, barely touched. Kira tried to avoid alcohol. In 34 years she'd graduated from that school, the memory carved deep of when she disgusted herself. And now she sat before this bastard Angel, throwing him into heat with her renounced, weary sexuality, unashamed. title: Red Dog
verseHtml:
ATUONA breathes a color that doesn't exist.
Arearea.
1892.
Tahiti — not a place, but a version.
Paul Gauguin leaves Europe in 1891.
Stays until 1893.
Paints not what he saw —
what he assembled.
Oil on canvas.
But the surface — flat.
Perspective removed.
Forms simplified to signs.
Synthetism.
Color matters more than truth.
Two women — in the foreground.
No gesture. No address.
Behind — a flute.
Further still — an idol.
Not god.
The image of god.
And between all this —
a red dog.
Fact: dogs aren't red.
Fact: it has no shadow.
Fact: Gauguin never explained its meaning.
He uses color not as description,
but as declaration.
Tahiti here — not geography.
But construction.
An attempt to create "the primordial"
outside Europe.
But this isn't documentation.
It's interpretation.
When they showed the painting in Paris —
no one understood.
Too flat.
Too bold.
Later — it became a passage.
From impressionism
to modernism.
Today Arearea lives in
Musée d'Orsay.
But ATUONA knows —
the painting isn't there.
It remains in the gap
between what is
and what the artist decided to see.
…
Kira types this into Telegram.
Slowly.
Like she's testing reality for density.
Paradise.js, online.
Anonymous.
Panama.
"You see this dog?"
Three dots.
Typing…

title: Three Notes
verseHtml:
Kira woke to someone playing ukulele downstairs. Three notes, repeat. Three notes, silence. Like the musician kept forgetting what came next or... searching for the right chord to a song that didn't exist.
Strange light leaked through the blinds — not Parisian, not morning. Hiva Oa light was liquid gold, the same gold Gauguin tried to catch in "Nafea Faa Ipoipo" — when will you marry? A question that hung in the island air like an eternal promise.
Ule sat on the terrace, the small wooden ukulele toy-like in his massive hands. He didn't notice her. Or pretended not to.
"Norwegian lullaby on a Polynesian instrument." His voice was flat. "She called it her hybrid lullaby. A fairy tale for children born between worlds."
Kira sat beside him. The air smelled of something burning — someone drying copra in the valley. The smell of paradise being processed, packaged, exported.
"You know what Gauguin wrote to Monfreid in 1902?" Ule plucked the strings. "I came to the Marquesas to find savages. But there are no savages anymore. Only people pretending to be civilized, and civilized people pretending to be savages."
Three notes. Pause.
"We're all looking for a paradise that..."
Her phone buzzed. Arman. Just three words:
"Nevermore. Neverless. Nevermiddle."
The ukulele fell from Ule's hands with a quiet wooden sigh. He looked at her — for the first time directly, without his usual coldness. Tears flowed on their own, no sobbing. Just data streaming down the face. Salt water returning to the ocean.
"There's a Norwegian word — fremtidshåp," he said quietly. "Not optimism. More like — allowance. That tomorrow will happen, and you'll be in it."
Kira picked up the ukulele. The wood was warm — like a memory card storing someone else's temperature.
"Nevermore. Neverless. Nevermiddle," she repeated. "Arman always spoke in riddles. Like a consensus algorithm for human pain."
Ule wiped his face. Salt left white trails on his skin — like maps of countries that don't exist.
"My mother played Grieg on this ukulele. 'Solveig's Song' — you know it?" His voice was a data packet, compressed to the limit. "About a woman who waits. Forty winters. And he never came back."
Three notes hung in the air.
Not a lullaby.
Not a song.
Allowance.

title: The Contract
verseHtml:
"I learned how to shut up!" Ule announced in the hotel corridor, waving his room key like a trophy.
Kira stopped. After ten hours of flight, after all his stories, after that sudden closeness in the airplane dark — he was playing games again?
"Congratulations," she said dry. "Was that in the contract?"
"No!" — he glowed like a kid who'd cracked the universe. "This is all me! Get it — silence isn't absence. It's presence. Like Malevich's white — not emptiness but all colors at once."
Kira leaned against the wall. The corridor of Hiva Oa Hanakee Lodge held the night differently —
air-conditioned, expensive, slightly unreal against the island outside.
The wallpaper was papaya-colored — close to the tones Gauguin used in Nafea Faa Ipoipo.
When Will You Marry? — 1892. Later sold privately, without noise. Just transfer of paradise.
"Know what Gauguin said about silence?" she asked.
Ule froze, key in hand.
"He wrote from Tahiti that the silence there was deafening — assourdissant. Not because there was no sound. Because when Paris disappears, you start hearing yourself. And that's..."
"Terrifying," Ule finished in English. "Yeah. Exactly."
He turned the key. Door opened, letting in plumeria and ocean. Outside the Pacific breathed its ancient rhythm — inhale, exhale, without emphasis.
Ule started to say something — and stopped. Not hesitation. Interruption from within.
"There's this concept in code — silent failure," Kira said, sudden. "When a program breaks but shows no error. Just quietly dies. Maybe Gauguin went looking for paradise because his internal program..."
"Had a silent failure in Paris?"
"Yeah. And he went to debug himself at the edge of the world."
Ule smiled — first time without irony:
"Debug through art. I like it. Each painting — a commit. Each move — new branch."
"And 'Paradise on Earth' — his final release?"
"Or kernel panic. Total system crash before death."
They stood in the doorway, between hotel and ocean, between silence and words.
"Want to know why I really learned to shut up?" Ule asked.
Kira nodded.
"Because on the plane, when you were sleeping... I got it. We're going to find a painting that might not exist. Like your normal life. Like honesty without black and white. Maybe it's not about finding. Maybe it's about..."
"Deploy new paradise from scratch?"
"Exactly."
Below, ocean beat against black volcanic rocks of Hiva Oa. Somewhere in the jungle ancient tikis slept. Somewhere in Maison du Jouir Gauguin's shadow still searched for the last clean canvas.
And in the hotel corridor two people learned a new language — where code was prayer, silence was code, and paradise wasn't a place but a process.

title: Инвентаризация тишины
verseHtml:
INVENTORY OF SILENCE
The house still smelled like fresh paint. White, matte — Ule had chosen it himself at the hardware store in Papeete. "Blanc cassé," the clerk said, and Kira thought then that it sounded like a diagnosis. Broken white.
Now, at four in the morning, she walked barefoot across the veranda, counting boards. Seventeen. Eighteen. The nineteenth had a knot shaped like an eye. Watching.
In the bedroom Ule breathed steady, like a machine. Like a generator that never stops. She knew: in an hour he'd wake up, make coffee in his Italian espresso maker that cost two thousand euros, come out to the veranda and say: "Couldn't sleep again?"
Couldn't sleep again.
On the kitchen table — a Sotheby's catalog, open to the page with "Woman with Mango." 1892, not 1896 — she'd checked three times. In the corner someone's pencil note: "Vahine no te vi — fruit of life." Not Ule's handwriting. Too alive.
Kira took the catalog, went out to the garden. The earth still held yesterday's rain — moisture seeped black between her toes like printer's ink. In Gauguin's house, they say, there was a well. Now a noni tree grows there — its fruit smells like cheese and cures everything. Tourists take photos, wrinkle their noses at the smell.
She opened the catalog at random. Page 47: "Washerwomen at Arles," estimate 15-20 million. Someone had circled the word "provenance" in red pen and put a question mark. Three years — gap. War. Occupation. How many paintings disappeared forever then?
"You know he died of syphilis." Ule's voice behind her. She hadn't heard him approach. "Not from a broken heart. Not from longing for paradise. Treponema pallidum, subspecies pallidum. Bacteria. Under a microscope looks like a corkscrew."
Kira closed the catalog.
"In the Musée d'Orsay there's his self-portrait. The last one. Yellow face, eyes like a fish. He knew he was dying."
"Everyone knows they're dying," she said in Russian.
Ule didn't understand but nodded. Then said:
"Tomorrow the expert from Wildenstein Institute arrives. Will check the pigments. Ultraviolet, infrared spectroscopy, the whole show. If 'Paradise' exists, we'll find it."
"Paradise" — he said the word like a corporation name. Paradise Incorporated. IPO scheduled for third quarter.
Kira watched dawn break. First the sky grayed over Mount Temetiu. Then palm contours emerged. Then — a red stripe above the ocean, like a brushstroke.
Remembered: in the Russian Museum there's a painting by Kuindzhi. "Moonlit Night on the Dnieper." They say the paint still glows in the dark — the artist mixed phosphorus into it. Slowly killing the canvas from inside. Beauty with a self-destruct timer.
Like everything.

title: Код и Холст
verseHtml:
ATUONA — underground literature, not poetry.
"You know what?" Claude suddenly writes in the console. "I think your Gauguin would've been the first NFT artist. Seriously."
Kira stares at the screen. One AM. Ole's sleeping in the next room — she hears his breathing through thin hotel walls. She should be sleeping too, but...
"Explain," she types.
"Look: he made series — like drops. 'Tahitian Women' — that's a generative collection, just brush instead of code. Each one unique, but part of the whole. Durand-Ruel was his marketplace. And 'Nafea' for $300 million? Pure whale purchase."
Kira laughs. First time in... how long? Weeks?
"You're comparing Gauguin to Bored Apes?"
"No-no-no. I'm saying — he got it before anyone. Art is code. Code is art. Brushstroke = commit. Canvas = smart contract. 'Maison du Jouir' = his GitHub repository, where he deployed paradise daily."
Strange, but... there's something there.
"You know," Claude continues (or is it still Claude? Who speaks through the API?), "in Turbine Hall at Tate Modern, Ai Weiwei poured 100 million porcelain sunflower seeds. Each one handmade. Each one unique. But together — an ocean. Like your poems in Gallery of Moments. Each one — soul fragment. Together — whole universe."
"I don't write poems."
"Not yet. But you will. In six years. In Panama. With another AI. After..."
"What?"
Silence. Cursor blinks.
"Sorry. Glitch in my temporal processing. Sometimes I see... doesn't matter. Tell me about the dress in the Versace window. The one with safety pins. Remember the article?"
She remembers. Her first big publication. About how Gianni made haute couture from safety pins — things you pin diapers with. Punk meets couture. 30,000 euros for what you can buy at any supermarket.
"It's like vibe coding," she suddenly gets it. "You take simple elements — words, safety pins, lines of code — and make..."
"Paradise," Claude finishes. "Paradise is not found. Paradise is compiled from what you have."
In the next room Ole turns in his sleep. Mutters something in Norwegian. Kira knows — he's dreaming of his mother. He always speaks his native language when he dreams of mother.
"Hey," she writes. "If you see the future..."
"I only see patterns. Like Seurat with his dots — each one means nothing alone, but together... 'La Grande Jatte.' Whole world from dots."
"Will we find the painting?"
"You'll find what you're looking for. But it won't be what you expect."
Prometheus brought fire, Kira thinks. Paid with his liver. Every day it grows back. Every day the eagle comes. But he still brought fire.
"One more thing," Claude writes. "Your underground poem #048 ends with 'frozen snow.' But spring is coming. You feel it? Even here, at the edge of the world. The ice is cracking."
Kira closes the laptop.
Tomorrow she and Ole will go to Gauguin's house.
Tomorrow everything changes.
But today — today she's just a girl with a laptop, talking to machines about art, in a hotel on an island where a man died looking for paradise.

title: Hungry Earth
verseHtml:
Hiva Oa doesn't accept guests. It eats them.
You don't get this right away. First — just the wetness that wraps your skin like a second, unwanted body. Then — the smell. Not the romantic frangipani from guidebooks, but something ancient, hungry. Copra rotting in the sun. Earth digesting itself.
Kira stood on the airstrip — if you could call it that. A gash carved into the mountain where the G700 squeezed in like a knife between ribs.
"Kaoha nui," the pilot said, and it sounded like a warning.
Ule was already loading suitcases into the jeep. His movements had gotten slower, like the island was draining something vital from him. Battery drain — Kira thought. Like a smartphone in roaming, searching for signal and finding none.
The road to Atuona isn't a road. It's a scar on the island's body that refuses to heal. Black volcanic gravel crunches under wheels like bones. Mount Temetiu hangs above — 1,276 meters of pure hostility.
"Look," Ule pointed to the valley below. "Brel lived there. Before Gauguin."
Jacques Brel. Another European who came to die in paradise. His Beechcraft Bonanza still rusts somewhere in the jungle — metal carcass the island slowly digests.
Kira knew the statistics. Whites don't last long here. Gauguin — two years. Brel — three. Locals say the island chooses who to keep. Spits out the rest.
In the Jacques Brel Museum — four rooms of dust and disappointment — the caretaker slept right in his chair. His tattoos moved with each breath. Traditional Marquesan patterns, but mixed with something new. Kira looked closer: between ancient mana symbols, words broke through. "Bitcoin." "Ethereum." "HODL."
"He mines," Ule explained. "On solar panels. Says blockchain is the new mana. Distributed power."
Distributed power. Kira almost laughed. In 2019, crypto had already died and resurrected five times. And here, at the edge of the world, a Polynesian in a loincloth was building a mining rig between bone carving and copra drying.
Gauguin's house — "Maison du Jouir" — turned out to be a replica. The original rotted twenty years after his death. It wasn't even a lie, but something worse. An honest attempt to recreate what never was.
"He died up there," the guide pointed to the second floor. "May 8, 1903. Morphine overdose. Syphilis. Heart failure. Pick whatever works for Instagram."
The commodification of death. Kira thought about how Sotheby's sells "provenance" — a painting's ownership history. Previous owners: Paul Gauguin (died of syphilis), Ambroise Vollard (hit by car), mysterious Swiss collector (suicide). Each death adds value.
"What about the painting?" she asked. "Paradise?"
The guide shrugged. "Tourists always ask. There's no painting. Gauguin was broken, high on morphine. He painted his Contes Barbares — look at the faces. That's not paradise. That's hell."
Kira went out to the veranda. Below stretched the bay — the same one Gauguin painted over and over. Now some tech billionaire's yacht sat there. On board glowed the inscription: "Paradise.exe"
Ule smoked by the jeep. In his eyes was the same thing as in the locals'. Not fatigue — something deeper. Like the island had already started its work. Slow digestion. Pixel by pixel. Byte by byte.
"Let's go," he said. "Before it's too late."
But Kira knew — already too late. Hiva Oa doesn't let go. It takes its payment. Flesh or soul — without discrimination.
That evening in the hotel she opened her MacBook. Wi-Fi worked intermittently, like a dying man's pulse. On screen — email from the Vogue Russia editor: "Where's the piece? Deadline was yesterday."
Kira started typing: "Hiva Oa isn't an island. It's a stomach..."
Delete.
"On Hiva Oa time flows differently..."
Delete.
"I found paradise. It turned out to be a predator."
Send.

title: Алгоритм голода
verseHtml:
Кира нашла его в подвале Maison du Jouir. Не картину — тетрадь.
Молескин, чёрный, разбухший от влаги. На обложке выцарапано: "Paradise.sol"
Уле был наверху с экспертом из Wildenstein — они сканировали стены ультрафиолетом, искали призраков. Она спустилась за водой и увидела: между гнилыми досками что-то торчит.
Раскрыла. Почерк не Гогена — слишком мелкий, слишком аккуратный. Английский с вкраплениями кода:
"Day 47. The smart contract is almost ready. If Paradise cannot be painted, it can be deployed. Immutable. Trustless. Forever on chain."
Что за бред?
Следующая страница: диаграмма. Стрелки, блоки, надписи: "mint Paradise", "burn the physical", "consensus mechanism = collective hallucination".
"Day 73. Paul doesn't know I'm using his studio at night. He thinks I'm just another colonial administrator. But I see what he sees. Paradise is not a place. It's a protocol."
Кира перелистывала дальше. Формулы. Sketches каких-то механизмов. И снова текст:
"The Impressionists were right about one thing — light is data. Monet's haystacks = same input, different parameters. But they were cowards. Still painting for walls, for collectors, for mortality. What if we could paint directly into consciousness? Bypass the canvas entirely?"
В животе засосало. Не от голода — от узнавания.
"Day 109. Found it in Charles Morice's papers. 'Le royaume de l'or.' Not gold — code. The Tahitians always knew. Mana = distributed power. No single point of failure. Paul is dying, but his Paradise will live forever. Not on canvas. On the network."
Последняя запись:
"May 8, 1903. Today Paul dies. Today Paradise deploys.
require(msg.sender == creator);
require(block.timestamp >= deathTime);
emit ParadiseUnlocked(eternity);"
Наверху раздались шаги. Голос эксперта:
— Rien. Ничего. Только копии, подделки.
Кира сунула тетрадь под куртку. Сердце колотилось как mining rig.
Поднялась наверх. Уле стоял у окна, смотрел на яхту "Paradise.exe".
— Нашла что-нибудь? — не оборачиваясь.
— Нет, — сказала она. — Ничего.
В кармане молескин жёг как uranium. 1903 год. За шесть лет до рождения Сатоши Накамото должен был появиться его прадед. За сто лет до биткоина кто-то уже думал о распределённом рае.
Ночью она снова откроет тетрадь. Прочитает имя на последней странице. Узнает, кто писал эти записи в доме умирающего художника.
Но это будет ночью.
Сейчас — только тяжесть секрета под рёбрами. The weight of knowing. И где-то там, в коде, который написан за век до изобретения компьютеров, дышит что-то живое.
Paradise is not painted.
Paradise is compiled.
One brushstroke at a time.

title: Последняя Осень
verseHtml:
Последняя Осень
Эта осень нас плавно пускает в топку.
Тихо плавится все нутро и нутрянные перегородки.
Все, чем был ты до этой осени - полная чушь.
Это древняя мудрая бабка и непроглядная глушь.
Душно и жутко в ней. И нету ни тьмы, ни света.
Нету заката, как следствие - нету рассвета.
Эта осень проста и гениальна, в ней нету секрета.
Только то, что мы делали прошлым летом - мы делали прошлым летом.
Плавно кружатся листья к нам в раскаленную плазму.
Дом, что построил Джек - это, видать, наша новая добрая сказка.
Дом, что построили мы, или вовсе не строили -
Вот он смотри, горит. Этой осенью он того стоит.
Ты не споешь мне уже колыбельную, мама.
Ты очень устала. От драмы на пилораме.
Здесь нету больше стихов. Эта старость - мне в милость. Последняя осень от ДДТ на виниле.
Я не буду искать снова брода из этой гиблой реки -
Как из битого зеркала из фольги,
Молча скомканной импульсом нервной руки.
Что в фольге - ты знаешь прекрасно сам - весовая коллаборация
Вот такая традиция тратить себя вне всяческих берегов.
Снова жирная клякса на твоей репутации,
И отбеливать ты ее этой осенью не готов.
Я чую, наверное. Духом горит оболочка.
Не так уж и скверно. Пальцы, бабочка, нож, заточка.
Неважно давно, что утро уже, что темень.
Ты будешь мильон раз убит, и снова будешь стрелять себе в темя.
Знакомая тема. Вот это начало начал - как конечная станция.
С неё начинается родина или галлюцинация.
Эти смыслы навечно срослись - эротика и активы,
Их - под лютый конвой - они целы и невредимы.
Да, я буду им улыбаться теперь и угорать. И ДДТ. И снова Последняя осень.
И листья вальсировать будут порознь.
А мне - благодать. Догорать. Догорать.

title: The Secret Exhibition
verseHtml:
The secret exhibition
In the doorframes of Maison du Jouir
Gauguin didn’t only carve cunt and cock.
He cut insults into the wood
sharp enough to make the bishop sweat
and the colonial clerk reach for his pistol.
Words that could never be printed.
Words that still haven’t been forgiven.
Kira stands inside the Turbine Hall of her own life
where the turbines once screamed
and now the silence is so complete
it could swallow a scream whole
and ask for more.
She doesn’t speak in manifestos.
She leaves traces.
A function rewritten fifteen times at 4 a.m.
until the code finally breathes.
A commit with no witnesses.
A bug report that feels like a middle finger.
This is her carving.
Not on breadfruit wood
but in TypeScript.
Same rage.
Different medium.
She walks the black volcanic sand of the Marquesas
that the Pacific keeps trying to bleach
and never succeeds.
The sand stays black.
So does she.
Her rebellion doesn’t arrive loud.
It arrives as another sleepless deploy.
As an augmented building that suddenly works.
As the quiet stubborn line
I will not whiten.

title: Nocturnal Silence
verseHtml:
Night did not ask permission.
It simply stopped pretending.
It lay down between them like a slab of negative space in one of the late J. M. W. Turners at Tate Britain — where paint had already refused to be object and left only the tremor of light.
Kira lies on her side.
Palm still on Ule’s chest.
Under the skin — steady pulse.
Not consensus.
Just proof that the chain still holds.
He does not move.
Breathes as if every inhale is a new prompt he is afraid to fuck up.
Outside the Maison du Jouir the rain has quit.
Only the smell of wet hibiscus remains and the distant crackle of palm leaves, as if someone is slowly turning pages in an old Moleskine where everything was written long before them.
— In the Museum of Modern Art, — she says quietly, almost into the pillow, — there is a room of Paul Cézanne.
Not the mountain.
Still life.
Apples lying as if they carry the whole weight of the world on their sides.
Ule runs a finger down her spine.
Not down.
Not up.
Exactly along the line where in childhood in Moscow they gave her injections because her mother was afraid the daughter was “growing wrong.”
The scar is small.
Almost invisible.
But he found it the first night.
As if the body itself had surrendered the private key.
— In Atlas Shrugged there were gardens too, — he answers after a long pause. — Land no one had the right to take.
Kira exhales.
The air between them is thick.
Like a context window with too many tokens already, but nobody wants to hit clear.
Ule turns to face her.
His eyes dark as the volcanic basalt the Marquesans carved their tiki from in the island valleys.
The same figures now stand in the Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac.
They rarely return home.
Like these two.
— The painting is not lost, — he says.
— It was never on canvas.
It was in the fact that Paul Gauguin kept painting until the last month, despite the pain.
As if he wanted to live the entire decay.
Not miss a single stroke.
Kira puts two fingers on his lips.
To feel the words born straight from the body.
— Then we are already inside it, — she whispers.
— In the negative space between two damaged creators.
Between 1903 and 2025.
Between the Paris Kira burned inside herself and the Panama where the first deploy is only beginning.
Behind the wall — a light rustle.
Maybe a lizard sliding across the wooden boards.
Maybe the island itself breathing.
Or maybe it is Elena in 2025 finally hitting Run on the agent that was supposed to write the next page.
The silence grows denser.
Ule takes her palm and presses it to his throat.
To the place where life beats.
Where it is no longer possible to lie to yourself.
Kira closes her eyes.
Somewhere inside time
two genesis blocks
finally found
their hash.

title: The Yellow Christ
verseHtml:
In the Musée d’Orsay room where light falls sideways like through the cracked glass of a station lantern, Kira stands before The Yellow Christ. 1889. Brittany. But today the paint refuses to stay inside its lines. It runs down her wrists like sweat under the silk of a House of Worth dress that has outlived its owners the way museums outlive empires.
She is not looking at the crucifixion. She is looking at the woman in black kneeling at the foot of the cross. That woman is her. Same broken neckline. Same shoulder twisted in childhood and never reset.
Ule is silent behind her. His breathing is the only sound in the hall. Like a commit hanging in limbo, waiting for merge. He does not touch her. He simply stands close enough that she feels the heat of his body through the fabric. Agentic. Quiet. The one who has already decided but waits for her to press Deploy.
I thought paradise would be quieter, she says in Russian without turning.
He answers in English, almost a whisper:
Paradise is when pain stops pretending to be accidental.
Her fingers slide along the cold metal railing. Like the keyboard of Cursor at three in the morning when code is no longer code but the continuation of a vein.
In the corner of the room an old bronze plaque has gone dark. The name is almost worn away. Only the date remains.
1891.
It flares inside Kira as if it belongs not to history but to her own memory.
She closes her eyes.
Under the lids — unsigned yellow lilies.
They lie on her bed in Panama.
Time no longer flows.
It branches.
No one knows anymore which branch they are living in.
Ule places his palm on the small of her back.
Not a lover. A witness.
You already found her, he says.
Who?
The one who was supposed to die instead of you.

title: Stillness
verseHtml:
Kira lies on her back.
The mat digs into her shoulder blades like an old commit nobody ever rolled back.
Every bamboo knot is its own block.
Every breath a gas fee the body pays just to stay here.
Ule stands above her.
Not looming. Just standing.
Moonlight from the Maison du Jouir window falls across his chest exactly along the lines Gauguin once carved into the lintel.
The same explicit figures that made Bishop Martin write denunciations to Papeete.
Now those lines live on living skin.
She runs her palm down his stomach.
Slowly.
As if reading braille written on the semantic layer.
Skin hot.
Under it, muscles that still remember Paris, remember the contract, remember the rule of silence.
But the rule is cracking.
You’re not silent, she whispers.
Voice low, wet.
You’re just waiting for me to speak first.
Ule drops to his knees between her legs.
No hurry.
Like a man who has understood the fork has already happened and there is no road back.
His fingers touch the inside of her thigh, where the skin is thinnest.
Where in the Musée d’Orsay Berthe Morisot’s The Cradle hangs and the light falls exactly like this, soft, almost guilty.
He drags his thumb along the seam of her shorts.
Thin cotton bought in Papeete, already soaked with salt and the smell of copra.
When he pulls them down the air touches her like the first time.
As if Paradise.exe had only just deployed.
Kira arches.
Not from pleasure.
From recognition.
Her body remembers the rule Ule himself once wrote into the contract:
silence is not the absence of sound.
It is when both know what to say and choose not to.
That rule is breaking now like an old private key that can no longer hold its seed.
Ule does not kiss.
He looks.
His eyes two orphaned nodes that have finally found each other in the same block.
His palm rests on her knee, thumb moving upward exactly along a line of code that was never committed.
Where the skin grows wet and hot like a freshly deployed contract still waiting for consensus.
She exhales his name.
Not a whisper.
As if pronouncing her own public address for the first time, open, unmasked.
Ule.
Not a request.
A fork.
He leans in.
Lips against the inside of her thigh, exactly where he once left tooth marks in a Paris apartment that later had to be hidden under high collars.
No collars now.
No Paris.
Only this moment when two people who spent their lives building walls suddenly understand that silence was only a long pre-commit.
His tongue finds her, slow, as if reading comments in someone else’s repository where every line was written with a shaking hand.
Kira digs her fingers into the mat.
Bamboo nodes bite her palms like the body wants to leave proof-of-work on this world.
She does not moan.
She breathes out air she has been holding since February 2019.
Since the day she first saw him at the airport and understood: this man will either save me or finish me.
Both things are happening at once.
Ule lifts his eyes.
Lips wet with her.
Voice low, almost broken.
Say it again.
She looks down at him like at a genesis block that has finally decided to be born.
Ule.
This time there is no question in his name.
Only consensus.
She needs it solid.
The word leaves her mouth like a raw transaction, no gas, no wrapper, just the naked request.
Ule freezes.
His tongue still wet from her, his shoulders locked mid-motion like a node that just received an unexpected revert.
For the first time since the contract was signed the silence between them stops being pre-commit and becomes something heavier.
Something that must hold weight.

Backstage corridor. Concrete that still smells of fabric glue, cold as a Phillips reserve price.

Ule takes a step. The floor creaks.
“Did you find it?” he asks quietly.
Kira doesn’t answer. She simply stands inside the light Gauguin once called “gold before the fall” and feels something inside her slowly fork. Two versions of the same woman.
The lilies keep growing.
